utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is open -- in session, rather. Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Tolimir. Good morning. I wish to welcome a good morning to the Prosecution, to the Defence, and all the people who are helping us in and around this courtroom. Good morning also to the witness's counsel. He's not there yet, but he will be brought in shortly. Since the President announced to us yesterday the Presiding Judge will not be able to be here during this first session, pursuant to Article 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the Trial Chamber is satisfied that it can sit. Pursuant to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I am charged with presiding this first hearing, first session. We will continue this morning with the examination-in-chief, led by the Prosecutor. Mr. McCloskey told us yesterday that he needs 30 more minutes to finish his examination-in-chief, and I hope that he will be able to do so within that period of time. Unless there is something to -- some issues to address right now, I would like to have the witness brought in. Are there any procedural matters? No, there are no procedural matters; no particular issues to address either. So, please, could you call the witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, Witness, Mr. Zoran Carkic. I wish you a good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind you that the oath that you gave yesterday, according to which you swore to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, still applies. So, Mr. McCloskey, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honour Judge Nyambe, and everyone also. I, unfortunately, think -- if we could go back a little bit. We need to -- we can stay in open session. And if we could go to 65 ter 7309. This will be the aerial image of Sjemec. And, Your Honours, for your knowledge, when we receive these materials, they come in electronic format, they get put in our evidence -- electronic system in another electronic format, and then they get transferred to e-court in another electronic format. And while over the years we've gotten much better, these -- they don't come out as precisely as we receive them. And so we did print out from the original electronic format a -- on photo paper, and I've shown this to Mr. Gajic and General Tolimir, and just so you can see it to get a better look at it, because I know it was of some discussion. And I would offer 7309, which is a replica of this, in evidence. It's one that doesn't have any markings, so that -- you can keep that, if you'd like it. I'll get a copy for the Defence as well. And I'll just show it to the witness briefly as well, just to see if he has any additional comments, having seen a better view of it. As you can see, it's the same image, but it doesn't -- it's not clouded by the yellows and other hues that, for some reason, end up on the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. The Trial Chamber has seen the picture, but I would also like the Defence and the witness to be able to see it first. The parties have looked at this photograph. Mr. McCloskey, what would you like to do? Would you like this basic photo, this paper photo, to be admitted in to file, or what would you like to do, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can just offer the electronic replica of the photo into evidence and people can just have that, if they want it, for their files. Unfortunately, I'm not sure what we can do with physical documents in this courtroom anymore. And it's not necessary, really. As long as we have the replica. And we'll always have this photograph if anyone wants to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber believes that it is acceptable, so this document will get a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 7309 shall be assigned Exhibit P2175. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Carkic, good morning. The photo is very similar to the one you spoke of. Is there any comment you'd like to make on it or any changes in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor. This physical form of the photograph is practically a pale copy of what we see on the screen. This is all that I can comment on. I cannot deal with the date, as indicated here, because I don't know when that was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I would now like to go into the subject-matter that we left off. And I believe that we should be in private session, based on the previous rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to thank Mr. McCloskey for finishing on time, almost on time, and we have now ended the examination-in-chief. Witness, you will now be cross-examined by the Defence. It is their right to put questions to you, to which you will have to answer calmly and courteously. General Tolimir, yesterday you've indicated that you needed eight hours for this cross-examination, and whereas the Prosecutor used approximately three hours. The Presiding Judge, Judge Fluegge, said, in English, that this evaluation seemed to be a little bit inappropriate, appeared to be or seemed to be slightly inappropriate. I will not necessarily use the same words. However, I would just like to make a comment. When it comes to time between examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence does not allow an exact grid in terms of how much time should be given to either parties. However, the Rules are clear in saying that it is the Trial Chamber which has to make sure that we don't waste time and that the principle of equity should always be applied, equity and equality between parties. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal varies from case to case when it comes to applying this. So when we have -- for instance, in the Krajisnik case, the Trial Chamber granted at each time 60 per cent of the time of the examination-in-chief to the Defence for the cross-examination. In the Martic case, the Trial Chamber granted the same time to the Defence as they did to the Prosecutor, so it was equal at a hundred per cent on both sides. Now, recently in the Karadzic case, the Trial Chamber set some criteria when it comes to spreading the time between the cross-examination and the examination-in-chief, and each time it is up to the Chamber to decide on the amount of hours of the time that would be granted to the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. But I would also like to mention the Prlic case. As you know, I also sit on that trial. And in that particular trial, we have the principle of equality. The Defence has a hundred per cent of time granted to the Prosecutor. And, as you know, in the Prlic trial, there are six accused. So when the Prosecution has, for instance, one hour, the Defence has also one hour, and the six accused have to share that one hour, for instance, in a case like that. So there was an appeal made by the Defence in that last case, but the Appeals Chamber did not condemn the Trial Chamber in the Prlic case. However, the Trial Chamber said that it is up to each Chamber and that they have the discretionary power. I would just like to remind you of this because, in fact, now I will give you the time for your cross-examination. I do not want to object to your request because, to my mind, up until now you have used very well the Trial Chamber's time. On many occasions, you have decided to cross-examine in a shorter amount of time than was granted to the examination-in-chief, and even sometimes you have even completely -- you have decided not to cross-examine. So I would like to say personally, to my mind, this, but I would also like to ask you to focus on relevant matters and to try to avoid repetition, knowing very well, of course, that you are defending yourself. So there you are, General Tolimir. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua, I greet everyone. I wish peace unto this home. I hope that this trial day and the whole trial end in keeping with God's will, not as I would wish it. And I wish a pleasant stay to Witness Carkic and his counsel, Mr. Stojanovic. I hope they will feel comfortable here and have a safe journey home. I will try to complete my cross-examination in as little time as possible and would really focus on those issues that are the most relevant to this case and use only the most important documents, such as those used yesterday and today. Whatever time allocation the Court decides upon, I will accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, since we are speaking the same language, you have a screen before you where you see a LiveNote of what we are saying, so I would ask you to watch the typing and wait with your answer until the typing of my question finishes, and only then start answering. That would be of great assistance to the interpreters. Yesterday, in the summary of the Prosecution, you were asked whether you had been a member of the JNA, and there was some confusion about the year and the time, but you've cleared that up. I'm not going to ask you about that anymore. Just tell me about your knowledge, while you were in Sarajevo, about the massacre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, first of all, I would like to greet you and wish you a long life and a happy life. I don't know the answer to the question of my own relevance as a witness, because I did not have occasion to see it, but I was in Sarajevo at that critical time when there was this exchange of Alija Izetbegovic and the attempt to implement the agreement that from the staff headquarters in the centre of Sarajevo, in the park, people be pulled out, and that Alija Izetbegovic, with his daughter, gets safely home. We, as our unit, received a signal --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You now say what happened, happened. Do you know what exactly happened, and what time, what year? Because we need it for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened, I think, in May, early May. Which date exactly, I don't remember, but it could be the 3rd or the 4th of May, 1992, when the column of people heading towards Lukavica was broke off, attacked. And on that occasion, a number of soldiers were killed. Many of them were captured. And from what we found out, they were later mistreated. My unit came into the area of Grbavica and Vraca on the morning of the 5th. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just tell me, if you know, who took those soldiers prisoners, according to your own information, and who killed those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mixed unit consisting of some JNA soldiers, conscripts doing their regular military service, and some reservists of the JNA. And the massacre was perpetrated, according to our information, the combined forces of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was there a single trial of anyone who committed -- who participated in the massacre of the column of soldiers who were withdrawing from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although I'm convinced that it is high time, because I listened personally to Ejub Ganic persuading Alija Izetbegovic that he was not in a position to lead, that he was in captivity, and although he was in that situation, he was practically being protected and kept safe by JNA units. And I believe there was involvement of the Bosnian politicians at the time that played a crucial role, and unfortunately Jovan Divjak was part of all that and he was in the field at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we learn in history that the assassination in Sarajevo triggered the war between the Austro-Hungarian Empire and Serbia in 1914, I'm sure we will be learning in history that the killing of the column of soldiers withdrawing from Sarajevo in 1992 triggered the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell the Trial Chamber: Was it a deliberate crime intended to start an inter-nation war among people who had, until then, been living peacefully together?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not qualified to make such judgements. I believe that if Alija Izetbegovic had any say in it, it wouldn't have happened. And I believe that there would have been more literate and better leadership on both sides. However, some other worse people got the upper hand. But, in any case, it was obvious that the whole thing had been planned. And before that, there was another incident that ended in a killing, the killing of a member of a Serbian wedding party, just before the war, just before the outbreak of the war. And the name of the victim was Gardovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you this because the history books will retain only the triggers and very few facts, so I want to emphasise this. Now, I now want to ask you about one of the triggers for the conflict in the region where you lived, for the specific reason that you were part of the brigade that entered Grbavica at that moment. Was that unit from Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit from -- was from the Military Post Box 1524. Those were leftovers of the 16th -- sorry, 216th Mountain Brigade, which came in its current composition to Sarajevo. It was made up of two incomplete battalions and battalion fire support, and the battalions were rump precisely for the reason that their Muslim comrades had deserted, openly or secretly, just before that in 1991. At any rate, all the Muslim members had left the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that the only active-duty unit based in Han Pijesak, and did it recruit all the conscripts from Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, from that entire area around Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the only unit of its kind, of its rank. And it had good manning levels before the war, and it recruited from Sokolac, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, Olovo, perhaps even Kladanj, Vlasenica, Milici. Most of the reserve soldiers - and I have to underline it's not a territorial defence unit; it was a JNA unit - most of the men were Muslims. While in the area of Han Pijesak, although I didn't know it at the time because it was kept secret, in the territory of Crna Rijeka there was a smaller unit of the JNA used to secure installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When your unit was mobilised, you said the Muslims were not present there. Can you tell us where the Muslims from, say, Han Pijesak and the surrounding villages went to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, they returned home. However, we had intelligence on Rogatica where, shortly after, units of the Patriotic League were formed. In the military sense, Rogatica was not organised regarding the JNA. Later on the Rogatica Battalion was formed for the very reasons I've discussed. Once it was formed as part of the 216th Mountain Brigade, and I did not belong to that unit, I was with the Sokolac Battalion, by that time there had already been Patriotic League units in Rogatica and the various local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said it was on the 4th of May. And on the 5th you arrived in Grbavica, near Sarajevo, with the rest of the force. Can you tell us why the JNA column was attacked on the 4th of May, when it was only on the 15th of May that the JNA began withdrawing from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I will draw a correct conclusion, but it is my strong impression that it had to happen because it was planned for it to happen. The Muslim leadership in Sarajevo had planned it. And similar things happened in Tuzla, following the same or a similar scenario. A similar occurrence also took place on the 4th of June in Zepa, following another similar scenario. It is true that in the large barracks in the centre of town in Sarajevo there was a JNA unit which had already been attacked and besieged. But once General Mladic arrived, things changed, and he made it known that he would not see that unit pull out of Sarajevo in shame. They were going to leave with their weapons. I believe they eventually pulled out in mid-May 1992. They went through the territory controlled by the Muslim forces and through our lines as well, finally leaving the territory of the then Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to be able to understand how the conflict came about in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You just mentioned the 4th of June, 1992. I'd like to have D91 placed on the screen, and then I would have a few questions about the 4th, but only after you have seen the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D91.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it on the screen. This is a criminal report submitted by the Interior Ministry of Republika Srpska and its Sarajevo Public Security Centre, against those who committed the crime on the 4th; that is to say, the attack on the JNA column in Zepa which was trying to reach the Zlovrh elevation. We have specific names, and the report states: "On the 4th of June" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see that on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't go through the list of persons. They are suspected of having committed this crime. And on the following page, there is an explanation as to why the criminal report was submitted in the first place. Under 5, we can see the name of the Zepa Brigade commander, Avdo Palic, and we have some of his associates on the list as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "On the 4th of June, 1992, early in the morning, several military vehicles and a fully-equipped battalion set out from Pale, over Han Pijesak, towards Zepa. They were members of the VRS, commanded by Major Dragan Suka. Their aim was to provide water, food, medical supplies, and other necessities required by VRS members for a unit the size of a platoon, which was in the area of Zepa, securing the military facility there, as well as the TV relay station at Zlovrh. Despite a previous agreement with the Muslim leadership in Zepa on securing free passage of the column to the facility and to Zlovrh, the Muslims, who were then organised in the so-called Patriotic League and the Green Berets, ambushed the column in a gorge near Zepa. On that occasion, 45 VRS members were killed." And we see their names. This is the explanation from the criminal report. The persons specified killed those listed in the statement of reasons. Do you know of this event, do you know when it took place, and do you know why the Muslims attacked the column once they had agreed that it could go through, and it was basically a humanitarian convoy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I wasn't in the area at the time, but I do recall, and later on it was going to be confirmed that it, indeed, took place on the 4th of June between Han Pijesak and Zlovrh, in the area of Budicin Potok. This is where the ambush was set up. It had a dramatic effect on the front-lines around Sarajevo. Many people who were killed on that occasion hailed from Pale. When their burial took place at Pale, some people manning positions around Sarajevo and Trebevic went to Pale. Being acquainted with the events, the Muslim forces seized of that opportunity to launch an attack along different axes, and in a matter of hours they broke through the front-line while most of the people manning those positions were attending the funeral of those killed at Budicin Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: As you said a moment ago, this was an act of murder of Serb soldiers who were part of a humanitarian column. Was this planned to cause fear, panic, and chaos by those who desired such developments in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. There is no evidence in the record, nor did we receive translation, that this witness has called this a murder. So far everything I've heard is "a military attack." And so unless he has evidence to that or that -- or he can state that it's his personal conclusion, that's fine, but to say that this witness said that or that there's evidence in the record is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir, you heard the objection raised by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Mindua. I heard the remark, but I was basically reading from the statement of reasons, where we can see that the Muslims had approved for the column to go through to supply water and food to the relay station, and that station was used by all ethnicities. However, they attacked them subsequently. I just wanted to know why it took place. Why did they breach the agreement and kill those people? And it is relevant for this witness because some of them had come from his unit. He also referred to the attacks which took place during their burial. Perhaps he can answer. I do not mean to simply disregard Mr. McCloskey's comment, but I was reading from the statement of reasons. I will later on refer to another criminal report which mentions people who were captured during that attack, and they describe the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I believe Mr. Tolimir has answered your objections. I believe we can proceed. General Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, at the time when you were a soldier, was there any information as to why there were constant attacks on JNA units, although they did not participate in combat? They were part of humanitarian convoys, supply columns, et cetera. Did you have any information as to why these attacks occurred on JNA members?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only draw my own conclusions. I suppose we can see that the same scenario is followed throughout, to carry out these attacks on the JNA. Most likely, the ultimate goal was to put forth a theory that the JNA carried out an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, although it's a ridiculous story. In any case, it seems that many believed. I believe that was the goal. And, of course, they also wanted to kill as many soldiers as possible. Such acts do not correspond to any sound military logic, but this is as it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we can see why it was submitted, and we can see how those who were taken prisoners were treated, as well as those who were killed. Let's look at paragraph 2: "According to existing indications, the main organisers of the treacherous attack against the said VRS column followed by the killing of some of those who were captured and wounded and whose bodies were mutilated and burned, were the following:" We see "Ramo Cardakovic" and others, including "Avdo Palic," command of the Zepa Brigade. In the third paragraph on the next page, the witnesses of the crime are referred to, the witnesses of the attack on the 4th, 5th, and 6th of June, 1992. In the next paragraph, it says while being seriously wounded, they could hear those Muslims who carried out the attack threatening to kill everyone. According to statements of witnesses, there was a seriously wounded VRS soldier who was completely helpless, who was killed by Nasko Lilic, et cetera. There is also mention made of how those who were captured were later killed and their bodies burned. Those of you manning the units in that area, such as your unit in Han Pijesak, did you know that there had been a massacre of that column trying to reach the relay station at Zlovrh? Did you have any information, as members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, information was known. We heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove this document and go to D92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll see it in a moment. This is a new, amended criminal report about the same event, for the crime of murder of those soldiers in Zepa. It was drafted on the 23rd of August, 1995. This is an amended report including 149 names of those who participated in the massacre of the Serb soldiers in Zepa. You can see all their names there, including "Avdo Palic," commander of the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 7, please, where the end of the list is. We will see what the report states in its statement of reasons. Apologies, page 9. We need page 9 to see the statement of reasons. We can see it now. Perhaps you can zoom in for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read out. It is difficult to read, but I'll do my best: "During the preliminary criminal investigation, the authorised personnel undertook a series of operative activities aimed at documenting the crimes set forth in the disposition of this criminal report." There were interviews conducted and statements taken from the witnesses and participants. And the Muslim fighters who took part in it were interviewed as well. This is why we have this new, amended report with 149 persons involved. Do you know anything about the activities undertaken by security organs in order to gain information about how the massacre occurred, when the Serb soldiers were killed in Zepa in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these documents. They were created in another period. In 1995, there was intense work on compiling data on crimes against humanity committed -- and committed crimes by Muslim forces against the Serbian civilian population and the military column that was moving towards Zlovrh, as well as investigations into other events. Statements were taken. As far as I can remember, a statement was also taken from Avdo Palic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This second indictment, does it confirm that 43 Serb soldiers were killed in an ambush, organised without any cause or outside of combat, by the Muslim Patriotic League? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I'm not able to see here, in the explanation of the document, that that number is mentioned, but we knew that it was 40-something persons, perhaps even more. At one point, it appeared to be 46 people, even, who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down the charges so that we can see the second paragraph on this page - thank you - which contains that number. Thank you. Can you please scroll down the Serbian version a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you can see here -- we're looking at the - first, second - third paragraph in the third line. It states: "On 4th of June, 1992, at the place called Riza, near the village of Brloznik, at the Han Pijesak-Godjenje-Stoborani crossroads, they carried out an attack on a column of military vehicles and soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, on which occasion they killed 43 VRS soldiers and officers, burned and destroyed a large number of vehicles and other materiel and technical equipment, and, in contravention of the rules ..." And so on. I'm sorry. Did you know that this happened? And you can see that this was stated by those who participated in the attack on this column .

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of it. And today, there is a monument on that place, and every year, at the anniversary, there is a memorial service in honour of those soldiers who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now look at what you gathered, and in terms of data about the weapons and preparations of the B&H army for fighting in that region, because you were in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document that you drafted. You will probably recognise it because it is your signature at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D162. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In e-court, can we now see that this is a document of the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, Organ for Security and Intelligence, dated the 31st of December, 1993? The document is titled "Intelligence and Security Information, Zepa-93." Are you able to tell us, according to your best recollection, why you drafted this kind of document, and what was the specific reason that this document was drafted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I cannot really remember. If it's a long, detailed document, perhaps it was drafted for the purposes of the annual counter-intelligence evaluations relating to the situation in the AOR. I can only see one page, but you said it was a long document, so that could be that. Or it could be a detailed analysis also. These kinds of analyses were done. It wasn't unusual to present an overview of all the intelligence data according to a set format.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 14 in e-court so that the witness could look at his signature so that we could identify the precise document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see your signature. It says "Chief of Section" or "Organ, Captain Zoran Carkic." Is that your actual signature that you placed above the typing "Chief of Organ, Zoran Carkic"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very similar to my signature. In that period, for some strange reason, I kept changing my signature. I had different signatures. But I do not dispute that I did draft analysis documents, and I'm not disputing that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you answer this question, please: In this evaluation or assessment, you stated the number of soldiers, the number of population in Zepa. Are you able to tell us, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber, what the parameters were so that we can see how big a territory was occupied by the enclave and how many soldiers were spread out in this area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation process began in the spring of 1993, the enclave, in the military sense, the way we viewed it from a military aspect, had about -- occupied an area of about 100 square kilometres, perhaps a little less, orthogonally. But in view of the terrain that is specific for that area, in our assessment we believed that it was some 115 or 150 kilometres of territory. The territory included two municipalities: that part of the zone belonging to the Rogatica municipality and the rest belonging to the Srebrenica municipality. And I'm thinking of the villages of Luke and Krusev Dol there, which are located east of Zepa, at a higher elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And in your analysis pertaining to the demilitarisation period in 1993 or immediately prior to it - actually, the analysis was done in late 1993/early 1994 - and then on page 4 you speak about the relations between Srebrenica and Zepa. And on page 4 of this page, I'm going to quote to you something, and then you can answer my question. The fourth paragraph begins as follows. We're looking at page 5. I was actually looking at the previous page. I made a mistake. This is paragraph 4, and I quote: "The life-line of the entire zone is the open corridor Zepa-Srebrenica. The corridor is being used on a daily basis for military purposes or pursuant to the requirements of the civilian population. The people from Zepa are trading cigarettes, tobacco, salt, and coffee with the people from Srebrenica." Are you able to tell us what you know about this corridor and what was happening in the corridor, focusing on military questions, and how was it that Srebrenica was receiving its supplies through Zepa? Can you please tell us what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was outside of the AOR of our brigade, but, in any case, it was in the zone of interest that I was covering, as the intelligence organ at the time, we compiled data about the meeting point between the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. They were already safe areas at the time that this document was drafted. They were subject to certain restrictions. There were UNPROFOR check-points. And based on what I know, there were UNPROFOR check-points in the Zepa zone as well. The passage was not permitted, especially passage involving engagement of soldiers in the corridor. However, information and the situation in the field will indicate that the corridors were used for different purposes, military, civilian purposes, throughout 1993 and 1994, until certain activities were undertaken to place the corridor under some form of control. Sometimes, this was sporadic, more or less successful, and then the corridor would be reactivated again. In any case, according to our information, during 1995 it was used, in particular, for smuggling and the sale of fuel, which was in short supply in the zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to call up any new documents. It's time for a break now. So I just want to ask you this: Was the Zepa corridor primarily used to supply arms to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our information also indicated that that was the case, especially in 1995 when there were more frequent contingents of weapons supplied by helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Mindua, if we're not going to have the break, I'm going to put my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Tolimir, it is just about 10.35 on the clock in front of us, so it is definitely time to have our first break. We shall stop now and resume at 11.00. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to greet everybody, as I was not present during the first session. Now the Bench is complete again. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago we were discussing document D62 and supplies of military and civilian resources through Srebrenica and Zepa. You said there were also air-lifts. Could we now look at D67. And when we have it, I'd like to ask you a question. And then you can tell us all about -- all you know about the air-lifts. There it is. It's an interim report from the Intelligence Administration of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their Anti-Electronic Combat Section, dated 13 July 1995, and it's called "Interim Report Delivered Through the 1st Corps Command to the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And in this document signed by Rasim Delic, they inform Alija Izetbegovic of all the steps they had taken to reinforce the military in Srebrenica and Zepa, and they say: "Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa: To start with, lethal assets and materiel and technical equipment were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities." And then: "Seventeen helicopter sorties were made, and in each of them a helicopter was hit. "We sent another helicopter with engineers and mechanics for one of the helicopters that was hit and had remained in Zepa, and repaired it successfully, and then both helicopters returned." The next page shows all the weapons they sent to Srebrenica and Zepa; that is, to Srebrenica via Zepa. You told us that military supplies were brought in to Srebrenica as well through Zepa, so I'd like to know: What was your information, the information and intelligence available to your brigade and your section, about military supplies from Zepa to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our intelligence reports indicated that there was an exchange of incoming weapons from Zepa to Srebrenica, that there were helicopter flights planned in such a way to bring supplies in one single flight to both Srebrenica and Zepa. We got that intelligence by monitoring radio communications but also by talking to certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that Muslims were militarily maintaining the corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa and they did not allow even the UNPROFOR to put check-points there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they used that corridor for military purposes, as well as civilian purposes, and I know that the situation was particularly sensitive at one of the check-points, I believe, manned by the Ukrainian Battalion around Bradovica [phoen] and Stublic. So from the northern border of the Zepa enclave, supplies were brought to the Srebrenica enclave. The UNPROFOR tried to intervene several times, but they were eventually forced to condone this smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the black-marketeering was rife and that one kilo of salt was sold for as much as 30 Deutschmark. Can you explain why the prices were so high, and if you had information about this smuggling and black-marketeering, and whether the UNPROFOR was involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have information. After the first convoys that arrived at Zepa enclave, there occurred significant changes in the attitude of the civilian and military leadership of Zepa. They were pumping up food and other resources. There was an operation called Package, which was probably a training operation by NATO, because they had brought enormous food supplies by land, and the Operation Parachute was hardly even necessary. We were not able to establish for sure that they received ammunition that way, but we certainly knew that they had received weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether those bare necessities, such as food, were brought -- were received in such enormous quantities by exaggerating the number of the inhabitants of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you had contacts with the UNPROFOR, did you try to point out to them what is happening, in terms of smuggling?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This check-point at Rogatica was a very delicate and tricky one in terms of intelligence and security, and we always insisted on inspecting all the convoys, whether they were organised by the UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations. And as a rule we would always find extra material or material of the kind that was forbidden or simply not reported in advance. And our brigade had positions facing these enclaves, which made our position very tricky. That's why the situation at these check-points and the problems there were very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At page 3 of the transcript, line 7, I believe the -- sorry, page 23, line 7, the Prosecutor asked you a question about when you dealt with that and you answered that upon request of Commander Pusic, you went to him to inform him of your knowledge about the enemy. Did that commander, having knowledge about the enemy, have the duty to inform me? Did he have the right to inform me when I was in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor asked you where it was, on page 23, line 13, you answered, in line 15, that it was at Boksanica, that command post was at Boksanica. Did you came [as interpreted] because you were summoned by me or because you had to have prior approval of your commander? Were you summoned by him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was summoned by my commander. Since I was carrying out my regular duties, and the main duty was to cover the front-line facing Gorazde, sometimes I went to that command post. On the occasion you are talking about, I believe I approached his vehicle to show him on the map the exact deployment of enemy forces facing our advance front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you came because you were summoned by your commander. Tell me, were all security organs in every unit subordinated exclusively and primarily to their commander and were duty-bound to carry out their orders, first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military structure, in terms of security and intelligence organs, was exactly as you describe. In the organisational structure of the units of the VRS and according to the system of subordination, our organs were subordinated to the commander within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were security organs at all levels subordinated to the commander, because the Prosecutor asked you yesterday who was superior to Beara? Did Beara have his own commander, just like you had yours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, because Colonel Beara led the Security Administration. And in view of the separation of tasks, he also had to be answerable to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday about the responsibilities and subordination, and my question is: To whom are security organs subordinated to? And we will later discuss the professional line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the chain of command, they are subordinated to the commander of the unit within which they work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As a security and intelligence organ in your brigade, did you have the duty to provide professional guidance to the corresponding security organs at lower levels, such as battalions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly one of my responsibilities to co-operate and help with the professional aspects of the security organs in lower-level units, not in any command sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said you were helping out with professional aspects of their work. But in terms of command, were you able to command security organs in lower-level units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, security organs were not quite the same as other organs. They were not able to issue commands. They could provide guidance, suggestions, proposals, requests, but they could not command units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that Beara could propose but he could not order. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the same principle applied at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I'm trying to be brief and skipping as much as I can, we have now completed this set of questions about duties and responsibilities. Could we now see a Prosecution exhibit -- no, Defence Exhibit D49. You were examined for a long time about Sjemec. Please look at the document again, and then I'll have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this would come up on the screen, I would like to put a final question to the last topic to the witness. I'm only talking about the relevant time in 1995. Who were the officers of the VRS who issued orders to you, personally? From whom did you receive any order; do you recall that? I'm interested in the factual situation and what you really recall. Who issued order to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat this again. At that time, there was a number of officers and high-ranking officers from the VRS, from the Drina Corps, and the Main Staff, and other brigade units. The task I spoke about, my general assignment in that period, was received from my commander. There were certain summons and calls from other commanders, calls for briefings, because my information was valuable to various commanders. Sometimes other commanders would ask my commander to summon me, and that's the typical situation in which I would go up there. In one case, which I discussed in private session - that's the 27th or the 28th, outside Borike Hotel - I was told the order was issued by the chief. To me, that meant that the order was issued by Ratko Mladic, and I didn't think twice. I don't remember receiving any orders from General Tolimir in that sense. And in that document where Colonel Beara addresses the brigade command, you can see he's not addressing me directly. He's addressing the brigade commander to let me carry out an assignment. So, in principle, I received orders from the command structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was not asking you about the specific incident outside the Borike Hotel, but in general, in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to the Borike Hotel as an example. In principle, commands come from commanders, meaning that I could have received an order from the commander of the Main Staff, the commander of the Drina Corps, or the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I saw you on your feet, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Carkic just made a reference to a document that he had spent a fair amount of time talking about this morning, and I think his answer would make a lot more sense to you if you would see that document. And I think it may help, be in response to your question as well. But, of course, that was in -- we were in private session during that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat that. I will have the chance to check all that, personally. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will take into account this request, and we will provide the document referred to by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that, in principle, commanders issue orders and that you could receive an order from any command level, be it the level of brigade, or corps, or the Main Staff. If an officer receives an order, an officer of the brigade, such as you, receives an order from the Drina Corps commander, what is his obligation vis-à-vis his own brigade commander and vis-à-vis the person issuing the order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, apologies. I was not a brigade commander. I was the security organ, intelligence and security organ. If I received an order from a certain command level, I am duty-bound to inform my own commander of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I had that in mind precisely. I apologise if I called you commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D49. It is on the screen, I believe. It has to do with the accommodation of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the first sentence, we can see this: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all POWs from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that space with pallets has been arranged for 800 POWs in the 1st Brigade in Sjemec." Since yesterday, during Mr. McCloskey's examination, you said that in 1992 and until the spring of 1993 there was a battalion of your brigade at Sjemec, can you tell us whether it was in the particular area of Sjemec referred to in the message, and did they use pallets for their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, the unit that was there in December of 1992 and later on in 1993 was billeted, for the most part, in the facilities along the regional road which goes through Sjemec. As regards the facilities discussed yesterday, the wooden facilities, they were not accommodated in those, but there may well have been some pallets referred to here there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this message provide the specific location as to where that accommodation was available or is only the general region of Sjemec mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall such details. Therefore, it is difficult for me to say which facility it could be. I only know of those facilities that were shown to me, and that's the only thing I can tell you anything about. However, these could have been specific buildings at that location, including the barns and the other buildings which may have been better equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I cannot decide on what questions the OTP will put to you, but I'm asking you this: Is this message intended only to inquire about the accommodation and to provide information about it, or does it also specify a certain location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind both speakers to pause between question and answer. We should avoid overlap, for the sake of the interpreters and the court recorder. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your brigade have technical capabilities of re-opening that facilities [as interpreted], if needed, in order to house POWs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we would have been able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the third paragraph, which reads: "If you send them to this sector, this must be done at night, using the transport and troops of the 1st Infantry Brigade." Is this a suggestion or only providing information as to what means are available to transport the POWs to a location unknown to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that is the gist or the meaning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Throughout the war, including this period in time and after that, at Sjemecko Polje, which you saw yesterday on an aerial image, were there ever any POWs accommodated there who were under the control of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Within a chain of command, is it allowed that a junior level of command should offer facilities to a more senior level of command that is within its area of responsible for use? Is this telegram suggesting that it has to be done or is it only providing information as to the opportunities there are?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this can only be seen as a proposal, as a possibility. This is no order, and the first, the very first, word tells you that. It is a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this proposal an offer to use the facilities of the brigade, because if it's a proposal, it has to be sent for approval to the commander? Do you think this is a proposal or merely providing information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically speaking, this is simply providing information, with a proposal in its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it a task of a security organ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Just, it seemed like we might be getting off this document. And I think it's clear to everyone, but just for the record, the translation we're getting is that this is the 1st Infantry Brigade that this is reference to, and, of course, it's the "1st plpbr," which we know is the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, which is the Rogatica Brigade. And so just because this is an important document, I want to make clear that that's understood on the record, because it's very hard for the translator to get that abbreviation. So -- and I'm sure everyone agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are referring to page 42, line 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't see it, but I'm sure you've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was -- Mr. Tolimir was reading something from the document, and it was not -- I don't know if he read it correctly or not. In the transcript, I see: "... using the transport and troops of the 1st Infantry Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was referring to. Thank you for getting that line and page. And I'm sure everyone will agree that it was the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, or the Rogatica Brigade, which is what the document actually says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, specifically, the transport and troops of that unit. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, sorry for this interruption. You put a question to the witness, and that was: "Is it a task of a security organ?" Could you answer this question, please, sir. No, this is a question to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to conclude my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it a task of security organs to secure accommodation of POWs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Whose task would it be within a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is something that the brigade command needs to deal with, including, most likely, the brigade commander and the Logistics Unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2D295. Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need 148, and it is item 295. D148, item 295. It is page 125 in the Serbian and 79 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, we'll see what the provisions have to say about it, and I'm showing it only now because I didn't want to suggest anything to you. We see item 295 of the command rules for the level of brigade and corps. It reads as follows: "Logistics support for prisoners of war includes the provision of necessary supplies and health-care. Provision of supplies to prisoners in prisoner stations and other locations, while they are under the jurisdiction of the armed forces, is organised by logistics and other organs in units which have captured them." This confirms what you have just said. My question is this: Was it standard practice in your brigade as well for the logistics units to take care of POWs, because security organs often comprised only two persons at a time and they couldn't handle it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the set of questions about the so-called Sjemec, which we have discussed. When Judge Fluegge was absent, we saw a document that was drafted by you, containing enemy information. You said that your brigade commander summoned you to convey that information because you were the most competent person in the brigade collecting enemy data. Tell us this, please: Was it your task -- was it your basic task to be assistant commander for security and intelligence, and were you supposed to acquire information on enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you forward all such information to your commander, Mr. Kusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday and today, several times you've said that your commander engaged you to monitor activities around Gorazde, which is on the opposite side from Zepa. My question is: Did any security organ have the right to dispute the decision of your commander for you to engage on military assignments there during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anybody dispute the decision of the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I was called out into the field, and to me this is quite understandable and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you because the translation was not concluded. Please pause between question and answer in the next question. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I don't know English, just reply, please. Did anyone, including the staff commander, dispute the decision of your commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell me if you went to any other assignment upon the permission of your commander, so that your commander would give permission every time you left for a new assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. The interpreters couldn't get your answer because you immediately started with your answer and the first part was not translated to us. Before you repeat your answer: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There may be a problem. We have: "Did anyone" -- So: "Did anyone, including the staff commander, dispute the decision of your commander?" I've never heard a staff -- what a staff commander is, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said, "Main Staff commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This was a valid correction. We have to come back to the last question of Mr. Tolimir. I repeat that: "Can you please tell me if you went to any other assignment upon the permission of your commander, so that your commander would give permission every time you left for a new assignment?" That was the question. Please now repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated yesterday, and I also said this in my statements, that I would often be informed, while touring the lines along the front towards Gorazde, via means of communication, that I have been summoned to come to Borike. But the approach and the principle, in essence, in that case, or in such cases, lay in the order of the brigade commander for me to be summoned, or possibly he received an order to call me. That is the logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carkic. Well, for the transcript, I see that we need to pay attention to each sentence, and I wasn't doing that up to now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we now look at 1D722, page 16 in the Serbian and page 11 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is an interview of yours to the Prosecution on the 23rd of February, 2011. Can you please tell us if this is the interview to which the Prosecutor also referred and to which you referred during your examination-in-chief, when saying, I said that to the Prosecutor? Is that the interview that you are thinking of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I referred to this document and also my statement yesterday -- my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the page I asked for, line 16 and 17. Can we look at the relevant page, please. It's page 11 in the English and page 16 in the Serbian. Can we also have these lines so that the witness can see them as well. I don't see the bottom of the page, the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you look at line 4 now, please. It starts with that row -- line on this page, and it states: "Zoran Carkic." And it states: "I got a task from the commander of the brigade especially to cover a part of the front-line towards the Gorazde enclave." And then later the investigator asked you: "And what did that mean, exactly?" And then you said: "It meant regular visits to the front-line, informing the members of the brigade about the situation at the other parts of the front-line, constant checking of security systems and security measures that are specific at the front-line, gathering of information about the enemy." My question is this: Since the brigade commander sent you, pursuant to his decision, to a location where he wasn't, so can you please tell us, during the Zepa operation, where was he and where did he send you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was at the forward command post. And again I say, my main assignment was to go to the opposite end of the AOR. These were positions of our brigade facing Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber why you had to be there and what was happening at that sector facing Gorazde. Can you please answer briefly so that the Trial Chamber could see why you were there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1995, in June, we had two major attacks from the Gorazde enclave towards our positions. And we were breaking through the front-lines, or our lines were being broken, and for that reason we had to engage men in order to retake that. There was fighting, there were killed and wounded persons, and preparations were ongoing for preparations of members of the Gorazde unit, Muslim forces in Gorazde, to link up with forces of the 1st Corps from Sarajevo and to ease the pressure on the front around Sarajevo and around Zepa. During the Zepa operation, we had a significant attack from the Gorazde enclave at our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you know, and probably do, could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether at the time there was a Muslim counter-offensive taking place and active combat from all enclaves against the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that happened before, before the Army of Republika Srpska responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at D62. Then we will come back to this statement of yours. Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we look at page 19 of this statement and page 13 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see here a part of your conversation with the OTP investigator, as a part of which he showed you some footage from Zepa and you were saying who you recognise. And then we can see, after 45 or 46 minutes, he asks you, I quote; he asks you: "Of course, it's me. I said I saw General Tolimir several times, and once in Zepa." And so on. While looking at the footage, he put that question to you. So, now, my question to you is this: Were you also involved in the Gorazde part of the front in order to resolve or execute the tasks given to you by the commander during the evacuation, and can you please tell the Trial Chamber what were the tasks that you were doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the interpreters concluded their translation of your previous question and we didn't have the answer of the witness on the record. Please pause. Please provide us with your last answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer should have been affirmative in that sense, because I believe that my commander should have received an order to summon me. And I think that is the principle that was functioning throughout that whole time. As far as my engagement was concerned, I don't know whether he called me directly or whether he received an order from perhaps General Mladic to call me, or -- I mean, not me, specifically. He perhaps decided to call me. I assume that I was called pursuant to the line of command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since the investigator first showed you yourself in the footage, how you were going in some buses, was your task to follow or escort the buses that were carrying out the evacuation in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the beginning of that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you said that citizens of Zepa went in two directions, one to Sarajevo and one to Kladanj. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber: What was your route in escorting them while crossing through the Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task lay along the Kladanj route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since there were two directions, Sarajevo and Kladanj, does that reflect the wishes of the population as to which destination they wanted to go to as long as the war was going on, as was defined by the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did correspond to the expressed needs and wishes of the citizens to decide for themselves where they wanted to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P4D5 -- P495. This is the agreement on disarming the able-bodied men in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not get all of the date. It was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll up the Serbian version of the document that we are looking at on the screen so that we can see 7, Article 7 or paragraph 7 of the agreement drafted by Rajko Kusic and certified by Ratko Mladic. And paragraph 7 says that: "Pursuant to the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949, and Additional Protocols of 1979, the civilian population of Zepa be enabled to freely choose their place of residence."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you please tell us if this was respected during the evacuation, although it was a problem for Republika Srpska to provide the option of two routes, two evacuations, and to provide escorts along those two routes for the population that was moving out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I witnessed that this was something that was respected. There was a choice available, either to go to Sarajevo or to Kladanj. And we had some help from UNPROFOR, who provided some of the resources in carrying out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I used OTP documents here, and I notice that in this paragraph 7 the word "for as long as the war lasts" has been erased, that they have a choice. I would like my Legal Advisor to show the original document with the agreement, where that part of the sentence was not left out. We need a little bit of time for him to find it. I have only just asked for it, and then we will show this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the meantime, my question is: Did any members of the Army of Republika Srpska decide where the population would go, and was there any kind of influence on the citizens while they were deciding where they wanted to go? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you remember if anyone was separated from those columns, from the buses, which also had some able-bodied men in them, and that was something that we could see yesterday during our examination-in-chief in the footage that was shown?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the last convoy to Kladanj, as we were coming back towards Vlasenica, we were stopped at one location near the village of Luke, on the road towards Kladanj. This was territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. There was a bus there that was supposed to return to Rogatica. That was the only case that I know of that a triage was carried out there, and a certain number of people were returned to Rogatica under police escort, military police of the Drina Corps escort, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you saw MPs from the Drina Corps, was this an activity ordered by the commander of your brigade or by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my commander had nothing to do with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If an assignment is carried out by the police subordinated to the commander of the Drina Corps, not the commander of your corps that you are able to train, are you able to make an assessment or know anything on that basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How do you know that this triage, this separation, was done at the orders of the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just saying it could have happened that way, because the military police of the Drina Corps was present. I'm just inferring that it was supposed to be on the orders of the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document yesterday, signed by you, where you wrote that a certain number of people separated by the military police of the Drina Corps had their money taken away from them and that I later ordered investigation as to who took money from these people, and, indeed, a list was made by the -- of these offenders. That was P1434. It was on the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P1434 again, the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before that is coming up on the screen, I would like to check if that was in private session yesterday. I'm not sure about that. Mr. McCloskey, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That is the 30 July document, and I believe it was. And so I think we should go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question that will be asked of the witness does not concern the matter for which we went into private session. I, therefore, believe we can stay in open session, with the consent of the witness and his counsel, of course. The question will concern the role of Mr. Tolimir, not the role of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please confer with your client, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Document P1434 should not be broadcast. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document where you stated all the problems that the detainees were experiencing. You stated, also, who they were. And, among other things, money had been taken away from them. And then it says, in paragraph 5: "During the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa on the morning of 20th July and the separation of able-bodied Muslim from the rest of the people, in the area of the primary school on the Divca [phoen]-Kladanj road, during inspection and search, some Muslims had money taken away from them. These people complained to General Tolimir and to me. They said it was done by some people who were commanded by a short, swarthy man." It's obviously, says the text: "Lieutenant Matic, who at the moment of separation of the Muslims came to the site and carried out searches in the school and in the school compound. "General Tolimir demands that this case be investigated and the money returned. "By authorisation from General Tolimir," says the signature, "chief of intelligence and security, Captain Zoran Carkic." Now tell me, was this the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue: That will not be a problem to broadcast this document. I checked again the transcript of yesterday; it was dealt with in open session. The last word of your quotation, Mr. Tolimir, is different on the text I see in front of me. The last sentence reads: "General Tolimir demands that this case is investigated and money found," and not "returned." This is the translation we have on the screen in English.
