I don't know the original text. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other important detail: In the document, the first sentence, it has the date of the evacuation. My document says "the morning of the 28th." In the LiveNote, it's got "20th," and that, I think, should be corrected. I don't know who made the mistake, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did. We didn't find the text in time. And the last word in question is, indeed, "found," not "returned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the headline of this document to see the date. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't -- he wasn't reading the headline. He was reading that section. It's page 57, line 7. It was the end of the document that he was reading from, and they just missed the date because it was so quick, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, this problem about the date occurred because I read too fast. Can you explain why this happened in the morning? Did the convoy spend the night travelling to this spot where Lieutenant Matic took this money away from people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please, to thank Mr. McCloskey for being so careful about every detail of yesterday's questioning which led us to go into private session at one point. I believe this date here, 28 of July, is the exact date of this event. And as for the part where it says "in the morning," as far as I remember, it was in the morning, because the convoy spent the night, had to spend the night, at a section of the road between Vlasenica and Divca. They had to stop because there was some combat going on in the broader area of Kladanj. Our AOR reports said that they had some advanced units, scouting units, close to our positions, and that's possibly the explanation for the skirmishes. The convoy was unable to go on, and that's why they continued in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, when I ordered you what I ordered, did you, when you signed this, write, "By authorisation from General Tolimir," write that because you felt it was necessary to emphasise it was on my orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the reason, although even without you being there and without anything you said I would have certainly taken steps to investigate. But since you were there, I did what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carkic. We will review the rest of this document in private session, including the list of persons who were wounded and the fair treatment accorded them. Now, since we are in open session, let me ask you this: In your view, did both of us, the security and intelligence organs, propose to the command that all adequate conditions be provided to the prisoners of war, under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On several occasions, I was able to see displays of your humanity, humaneness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then there's this issue of the representative of the ICRC who came to list all the detainees in Rogatica. The Prosecutor showed you a 65 ter document, 07304. Let's look at it again. While we wait, let me say, it's a document from the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, dated 30th July. It was sent also to a sector of the Main Staff, and it was signed by Zoran Carkic. We can now see it. And right at the top, below the heading -- and the heading says: "Visit to Prisoners of War in the Rogatica Military Holding Centre by the ICRC Delegation: Report."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't broadcast the document. And I will protect the identity of the people who are in detention, as the Prosecution asks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "Around 1000 hours on 30th of July, the prisoners of war in Rogatica were visited by an ICRC delegation from their Pale office, comprised of:" And then they list the members of their delegation. We can skip that part. You can see that you wrote this report. And if we turn to page 2, you say -- let's look at line 1: "I informed the delegation about all the details they wanted to know about. There were also physicians attending medical examinations performed by our physicians." Does this confirm your earlier statement? Did you, indeed, write this document, and were you an eye-witness to this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I don't remember all the details, but I remember that they came, that people were registered. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the examination-in-chief, you were asked several times whether you registered the detainees, whether you reported them. Did you report all the prisoners who were being held at this location in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you again. We didn't receive the interpretation of the answer because you started with your next question earlier. Could you please give us your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text of this document testifies that they were registered, they were reported to the ICRC commission, in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was: "Did you report all the prisoners who were being held at this location in Rogatica?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I think they were registered, those in the Military Holding Centre Rasadnik in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document. And whatever we want to ask about it in private session, we will ask once we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7304 shall be assigned Exhibit D211. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have P51 next so that we can see the original text of the agreement, because in the document we just saw a moment ago, some important facts are missing. Sorry, could we have D51 in e-court. Thank you. Please zoom in so that we can see item 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949, and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." This is a very important part of the sentence: "while hostilities continue." My question is this: Does it mean that under the agreement, that evacuation, that transfer, was only in effect while hostilities continue; in other words, that it was not foreseen as a permanent state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber whether, in the area of the former enclave of Zepa, there are now Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowadays, yes. Some of them returned. Perhaps some 300 houses were reconstructed. But most of them are only there on weekends. There are very few who reside there permanently in Zepa, so that figure is actually rather small.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it indicate that after the hostilities, as foreseen by the Dayton Accords, which followed the evacuation closely, they were free to go back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was understood. The returnee project was initiated and was underway throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is still underway. However, only the issue of property return was completely resolved. As for the physical return of the people, that is still something that is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D62 in order to introduce the next topic, which has been touched upon only briefly. It has to do with combat activities from the enclave out, immediately preceding the events discussed here, which resulted in the signing of the agreement we saw a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see an Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina document. It came from the 285th Light Brigade of Zepa, Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade. It was sent to the 2nd Corps Command of the Army of BiH and to the 28th Division Command in Srebrenica, to Ramiz Becirovic. My question is this: Can you tell us why this document, authored by the Zepa Brigade commander, was sent to the 28th Division Command in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it because we had precise intelligence, and we know that the 285th East Bosnia Light Brigade in Zepa was part of the 28th Division. All those units came into being in mid-1994, and their growth continued until, in 1995, they were fully capable of executing combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the cause for those units to build up to the level of brigade? What was the basic impetus?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was a reorganisation in the system of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Obviously, some procedure was followed, as well as rules, which were developed during the war, itself. What is the most interesting, though, is to note that such level units, division-level units, were created in the enclaves that were supposed to have been demilitarised back in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The amounts of weapons which arrived in the so-called demilitarised protected areas, did that affect the growth of these formations to such units capable of performing activities both inside and outside those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were organised activities from the enclave, as well as attacks, immediately prior to the VRS deciding to halt such occurrences and to intervene?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early July or in late June, I know for sure that there were several sabotage groups from the 285th Brigade from Zepa which started moving along a long axis towards VRS territory. They went outside the demilitarised zone in combat deployment, and they carried out sabotage operations in a wide area, with the aim of attacking not only the Main Staff, but also to cut off the road between Han Pijesak and Vlasenica. That was the size of the area that was encompassed in their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the document. Let me ask you this: Did their activities from the enclave increase alongside the general Muslim offensive carried out against the VRS units and RS territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. We knew -- we had information that they were ordered to launch attacks so as to relieve the pressure of their forces who were -- which were deployed at Treskavica and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the combat report, itself, of the Zepa Brigade: "Based on the order of the deputy commander of the 28th Division, Srebrenica, Major Ramiz Becirovic ..." and we have the strictly confidential number "... of the 28th of June, 1995, on measures to be taken for the execution of sabotage actions aimed at inflicting losses upon the aggressor in terms of troops and equipment and, in general, at turning the Chetnik forces away from Sarajevo." In the third paragraph, we see this: "Form a number of sabotage groups of between a squad to reinforce platoon strength and dispatch them deep into the temporarily occupied territory for the purpose of inflicting on the aggressor as great losses as possible, in terms of troops and equipment, and tying him down, with the new forces he requires ..." Down in the text, there is a reference to nine such groups that were formed and sent to different areas in the RS. My question is this: Did you have any information about it, and did you notify your superiors, that is to say, the superior command and your own commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have such information perhaps a fortnight before it actually happened. We had received information from the Drina Corps that something was going on, in the military sense, which had to do with the enclaves. We only received firm confirmation of it once it began developing. We knew of Srebrenica [as interpreted], and I know that managed to come to the outskirts of the village of Karaula [Realtime transcript read in error "Kralj"], close to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped Mr. Tolimir. He was putting the next question. We are running out of time. It's time for the second break of today. We adjourn, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was informed that Mr. Stojanovic wants to raise a matter. Mr. Stojanovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, I have an administrative issue to raise. During the break, I spoke with Mr. Carkic about the obligations and problems we are facing in Bosnia, where we came from. I was asked by Mr. Carkic to convey his position to you. He lives with his elderly mother, and he's taking care of her. He also has professional obligations on Monday. And our kind request would be to conclude with his testimony today, if in any way possible, although I have been advised that there is a possibility to continue tomorrow. So if we could complete it by the end of this week, that would be very appreciated. I also have professional obligation before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the Dusko Jevtic et al. case. I was supposed to give my closing argument -- opening statement on Monday, although I have asked already for it to be postponed. In any case, we have significant professional obligations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if it's not too much trouble for everyone involved, including the Chamber and the parties, we would kindly ask you to conclude this week, if in any way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe the best solution in this case could be to have a session tomorrow in exchange for Monday, for example. Then on Monday we might have a day off that could be used for preparation for the following witnesses, and Defence preparations in general. We hope there is an administrative possibility to sit tomorrow. As far as we know, at least one courtroom is available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've, unfortunately, made our plans for witnesses next week based on the estimates, and so how changeable all that is, I don't know. And given that General Tolimir has several more hours that he should be able to use, I don't really see a way out of it, aside from plugging ahead with our schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about rescheduling to have a hearing tomorrow instead of next Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That, we'd have to check. As you know, we have been dealing with the next witness on that. It may be changeable for that witness. And that is the first I've heard of this, so we haven't -- we don't have any information on it. But we can -- we can see. But that does create a big problem in the scheduling because it comes so out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's true. On the other hand, it was very clear that it would not be possible to conclude the testimony of this witness today. This is obvious. Mr. Tolimir has used a little bit more than two hours up to now in cross-examination. He has several hours more, and you will for sure re-examine him. It's only the question if it happens on Monday or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And Mr. Thayer sent out a revised schedule based on precisely what you said, and of course that has Mr. Carkic's continued cross on Monday and continued cross on Tuesday, given the general's estimates, which I think is fair, and Mr. -- the next witness on Tuesday as well. Hopefully, we'll -- we'd get him in there. And that's -- we'll check with Mr. Thayer, see how changeable that might be. And if you're open for Friday, that's, of course, the other big question. We will make ourselves open for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We just checked among the Judges. We will not be able to sit tomorrow. We will not be able to sit tomorrow. If it's possible to conclude cross-examination and re-examination in 35 minutes, that would be fine, but I don't think this is achievable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are putting a question to me in order to satisfy Mr. Carkic and his counsel, I suggest we conclude today with everything I have. I didn't start examining right off from the start today because it was still the Prosecutor's turn, but I'm more than willing to cut things short. If in any way possible, we want to have an extended session to conclude with everything. However, I don't want any fingers pointed at us, because the Prosecutor envisaged redirect, in any case, on Monday. We're trying to be as flexible as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This could be another possibility, another option: To have an extended sitting today to enable you to use as much time as possible during your cross-examination. In the meantime, the Registry could check if there is a courtroom available for an extended sitting. But not to waste more Court time, you should continue your cross-examination, and we will decide at the end of this session, in more than half an hour, how to proceed. Please continue. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be brief. Page 66, lines 16 and 17 of the transcript, I believe the witness mentioned Visnjica and another location, rather than Srebrenica and Kralj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 66, lines 16 and 17. We see here the answer was about information: You received information a fortnight before it actually happened. "We received information from the Drina Corps that something happened." And then the following sentence is recorded: "We knew of Srebrenica, and I know that managed to come to the outskirts of the village of Kralj, close to Han Pijesak." Are you referring to this part of the transcript, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, Precisely. The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what was wrong with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should read: "We knew about Visnjica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will check it with the witness. Sir, do you recall having said something to that effect, and which municipalities or villages did you mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said that a few days before it happened we had some information from the Drina Corps that from the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, something was to be expected. General Tolimir asked me what was it that we found out, and I told him that we had some information, following the events, about the destroyed village of Visnjica and an attempted attack on the village of Karaula, and not Kralj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please look at the transcript now. We see "Visnjica" and "Karaula"; is that the right spelling of this -- the name of this village? Thank you very much. I think we have it now clear on the record. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have D62 again. We had it at the end of the last session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I had a different image a moment ago. We can see it on the screen, and we see that nine groups were formed in order to engage different facilities, such as Han Kranj, Rijeka, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just before the nine groups, it says: "Form a number of sabotage groups of between a squad to reinforce platoon strength and dispatch them deep into the temporarily occupied territory for the purpose of inflicting on the aggressor as great losses as possible, in terms of troops and equipment, and tying him down, with the new forces he requires, on a line over 20 kilometres wide." In item 9, we have the village of Visnjica you mentioned a moment ago. My question is this: This is Avdo Palic's document. Was his Zepa Brigade sufficiently strong to be able to form nine sabotage groups in order to tie down VRS forces along a 20-kilometre front-line, causing losses, in keeping with the orders of their superior command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious from the document that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We just saw that the ninth group was to attack the Chetnik fortification and the units in Visnjica settlement. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was they were supposed to destroy the village of Visnjica, not the units stationed around. Their objective was the destruction of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have information that the village was destroyed, once it was destroyed; and did the UNPROFOR know about that, because you had contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we were informed. We received reports about the outcome of this attack by units of the Drina Corps -- from units of the Drina Corps, and I believe the operation of mopping up the terrain lasted for days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph, which says around 40 Chetniks were killed. Could we scroll up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Before you move to the next page, I would like to clarify one answer of you. You said: "Their objective was the destruction of the village." I read here, Group 9: "The area of Visnjica. Target the Chetnik fortification and units in the Visnjica settlement." How -- I would like to hear your interpretation of the words "fortification" and "units."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's quite clear; there's no call for special interpretation. It's clear what "Chetnik fortification" means, as well as "units around Visnjica village." But my information was that the only thing that was there was a village. There was no unit inside the village itself or at the watch tower. Visnjica is part of Milici municipality, or perhaps even Srebrenica municipality - I'm not sure - but everybody talked about the burning of Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was there a Serb fortification? You said there were no units, Serb units, in the village. Was there a kind of fortification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the deployment of forces in that area, and I can't say anything with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now please continue with the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now you see the last paragraph. It says forty Chetniks were killed, a considerable amount of weapon and ammunition had been seized, even one soldier was captured, by the name of Velimir Mrdjan, from Glamoc, and that he is in Zepa receiving treatment, which means he was also wounded. Could you tell us now: Were these such forceful activities that a unit from inside the protected area was engaged and the attack reached the Main Staff, because this man was part of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that dozens of men were involved. Mrdjan was captured and wounded. I know there were deaths. I don't know the exact number, but quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll show a document now, showing you the number. But while we're looking, let's look at document D52, showing that it was a large number of men killed. D52, like the previous document, it's from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's their own report, their own information. So it's not originating from the VRS. There's no fabrication. Let's see the first bullet point: "Sixty Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unverified information, the aggressor has suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." Then the following paragraph says: "In the populated area of Visnjica, a large amount of ammunition was found, but because the men were exhausted, we did not manage to seize more of it. So it was destroyed along with all the features and buildings that the aggressor could possibly use for military purposes." Does this mean that the village was torched?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that some men were killed, whether 30, 40, or 60. I know that others were wounded. I know that additional forces of the VRS and the MUP had to be engaged to search the terrain and to bring back this territory into the demilitarised zone. And as far as Visnjica is concerned, it was outside the area of my brigade. But I heard the village was destroyed. I heard nothing about ammunition or military installations. I understood, from what people were saying, that these were civilian buildings, residential houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at the document before you, and look at the date, "8 July, 1995." Tell the Trial Chamber whether that was on the eve of the critical events and before the attack of the VRS on this enclave from which these attacks originated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the date, I can see it was before the Stupcanica operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D145, relating to the period one month before the events in Zepa and Srebrenica, 24 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It speaks about the activities of the enemy: "We hereby inform you of the following reports concerning the intentions of the enemy." It's addressed to the commander of the 67th Communications Regiment: "We hereby submit the following information on the enemy's intentions:" I quote: "At 0200 hours on 23rd June this year, a unit of approximately 300 soldiers headed out from Srebrenica, led by Ibrahim Mandzic, commander of the 280th Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade; Vejiz Sabic, commander of the 284th Brigade; and his deputy, Semso Salihovic; along with a guide called Zoran Cardakovic. This unit's task was to attract the VRS forces in order to secure safe passage for Naser Oric." And third down, it says: "According to our information, the return of Naser Oric is connected with plans to commence combat operations from the Srebrenica enclave, which, supposedly, is conditioned by the possible taking of the Vis elevation in the Serbian municipality of Kalesija by the Muslim forces ..." And then it says: "Following this, it is supposed that combat would begin from the direction of Kladanj towards the VRS defence lines in the zone of responsibility of the Vlasenica Brigade, when the units from Srebrenica would insert themselves towards Konjevic Polje via the sector of Buljim and Milici." And then turn the page and look at the last --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused please wait until we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "The 65th Motorised Protection Regiment will ensure the necessary co-operatio with MUP at the Han Pijesak Garrison." Signed: "Major General Zdravko Tolimir." Was this the attack you described, and whether these people mentioned here were from the Zepa Brigade or the Srebrenica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said a moment ago when I said we had certain advance reports before these attacks at Visnjica and in the direction of Suva Rijeka. It is precisely reflected in this document. But we didn't receive it directly from you; we received it, of course, from the command of the Drina Corps. In any case, we had occasion to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether the 65th and the 66th -- 65th Protection Regiment and the 67th Communication Regiment were in that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch this question. Would the accused slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get everything. You were -- should repeat your question, please, and a little bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Muslim forces out of the so-called demilitarised zones, Zepa and Srebrenica, attack the location where the Main Staff of the VRS was based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the reports and documents of the Zepa Brigade, the base and the Main Staff was in the epicenter of these events. When they attacked with their sabotage groups, we can see that the area of the Main Staff was in the centre of their activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D53. And we have no time to introduce any further documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I take this opportunity to make the following proposal about the further part of the hearing. It could be possible that we have an extended sitting today. If we continue until 2.00, then we have half an hour, then a break of half an hour, and a final session from 2.30 to 4.00 in the afternoon. I would like to put that to all participants here, and you may check it while we are continuing with the questioning. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can be here for that. And Mr. Thayer informs me we can move our witness on to Monday that was scheduled for Tuesday. It may create a gap in the week. We're trying to fill that with someone else we put off. But we can manage it, though. This is a -- what's come up here was very predictable, and this is quite a bit of movement for something that I'm not sure is worth it. This is an important witness. And to rush it like this for this reason, I'm -- I mean, we'll do it, but I'm not sure it's worth it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We're only proposing this scheduling because the Defence indicated they wanted to stop as soon as possible, and this is quite in contradiction to their own time estimate. And, therefore, I wanted to find a way to please both the Defence and the witness and his counsel. The other possibility is still that at a later stage the witness has to come back for continuation of the cross-examination. But I leave it to the Defence. You are not under time pressure, as you know. You should decide for yourself, Mr. Tolimir, if you want to have an extended sitting today or if the witness should be called again for a continuation of your cross-examination, re-examination, and possible questions by the Judges. You should decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will finish today, in the regular hours; at least the questions which do not require private session. In the segment between 2.00 and 4.00, we would deal with the issues that require private session and also leave enough time for a redirect in order to free this witness to accommodate his prior commitments. I don't think there's any need for re-calling this witness, because if any issues remain outstanding with him, I will deal with them with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. McCloskey raised some concern, and I share this concern. There is no problem to re-call the witness. If you said you need the time, you should use the time for cross-examination. You are not under pressure. Now you said you want to finish in the regular time. That would mean in 10 minutes. This is not possible, and I would not suggest it to you. "We will finish today in the regular hours," you said. I took it that you wanted to finish in around 15 minutes. Or including the additional time this afternoon? I would like to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I meant that in the regular hours I can finish with the open session part. And then in the extension that you announced, we could have a private session in which I would deal with the rest of my examination and Mr. McCloskey could do his redirect. I would not have a problem that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. It's your decision, and we would proceed accordingly. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, please give me brief answers, or yes-or-no answers, as you deem fit. Here you see a document dated 17 June 1995, a document from the Army General Staff, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's an order written by the chief of staff of the 2nd Corps, Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic, and he sent it to the 28th Division of the Land Forces. It says: "Pursuant to verbal orders from the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, Rasim Delic, and following the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the broader area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the aggressor forces," that's how they call us, the VRS, "Command of the Protection Regiment in Han Pijesak is holding part of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa." And the order is: "Execute all preparations; to execute offensive combat operations; to liberate the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Stretch out the aggressor forces and inflict maximum losses on them." In this order, can we see that they are planning a broader operation, where he orders the liberation of Bosnian territory, including the protected areas Srebrenica and Gorazde, the area where you were engaged?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had reports of these plans. We had advance notice, perhaps even six months in advance. So we were not surprised by this order. It fits in with the plans of the newly-formed units of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm wrapping up this set of questions, and I'll now move to another topic you are familiar with, namely, the convoys. We'll now look at 1D454. I'm saying you're familiar with the subject because you were appointed by your command to liaison with the UNPROFOR, and the units of your brigade monitored the check-points through which supplies were transported to the enclaves. This was written on the 27th of February, 1995, by Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in so we can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Minister, Dr. Hasan Muratovic." I'll read what he says. I'm reading this bit, where it says: "To President of the municipality of Zepa. "Dear sir, we have received the UNHCR report on humanitarian aid deliveries to Zepa for the period 1 December 1994 to 15 February 1995. The report shows that 85 per cent of the aid was successfully delivered, on average, which is satisfactory. This is the breakdown of the items delivered:" And then follows an itemised list, with amounts indicated in tonnes. The last paragraph reads: "From the above, one can conclude that the UNHCR is supplying Zepa relatively well, and we continuously monitor this and maintain permanent contact with them." Signed: "Dr. Hasan Muratovic, Minister." Did you have the same reports, that Zepa is supplied regularly and well with the necessary amounts of food, and even greater than necessary amounts of food, enough to even sell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D454 shall be assigned Exhibit D212. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone. Sometimes we can hear your conversation with your assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. Could we have 1D703, and it is a document my Legal Assistant pointed out to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at the document. I will read the title only. It is a list of humanitarian aid delivered to the Zepa enclave in 1994 by the UNHCR, ICRC, and other organisations. We can see the breakdown per month. Perhaps you can offer your interpretation of the quantities shown, and, if possible, corroborate that with the information you had at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, we did analyse the humanitarian and other assistance to the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde. From time to time, we informed the Drina Corps of our information. I believe the information was well sorted out, and the only thing I can tell you now was that it concerned enormous quantities of food and other material which had nothing to do with food, including medication, equipment, blankets, footwear, seeds, which, of course, are related to food, as well as other material for daily use. In any case, there was a lot of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This breakdown was drafted by Captain Novakovic, as we can see at the bottom of the document. Can you tell us who he is? Did you know him? Were you in contact with him regarding the supply of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I cannot recall Mr. Slavko Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Drina Corps have a person who was constantly in touch with the units whose areas of responsibility were to be traversed by humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it perhaps this Slavko Novakovic, the captain, who was in charge of it in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I cannot recall the person's name, but I know for sure that the Drina Corps did have an UNPROFOR liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Your Honours, which is 1D703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D703 shall be assigned Exhibit D213. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 05284 in e-court. It is from the OTP's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit D209. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the supply in 1995, immediately prior to the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa in March and April. We see the quantities expressed in tonnes, and we can see which enclave received what quantities. Can you comment the figures, as compared to the number of the population, and what you knew about the enclaves bordering on the area of responsibility of the Rogatica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, our information was that the local leadership in Zepa, including both civilian and military authorities, was presenting figures that were too high, in terms of population, to these humanitarian organisations. I think for Zepa, they operated with the figure of up to 16.000 inhabitants at the time, or around that figure. In our estimates, there were only between seven and seven and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that they provided figures twice as high to the international humanitarian organisations providing supplies to them, whereas their real numbers were only half of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. We even had indications that the UNHCR was aware of the figures not being correct. In any case, they supplied them as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 1D641. It is a report on the abuse of humanitarian assistance, signed by the same person, Slavko Novakovic, captain, from the Drina Corps. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you'll see later, it was drafted on the 14th of February, 1993 -- 1994. Having in mind this report on the abuses of the mandate of international organisations, which is something you addressed during the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, can you tell us what were the most common types of abuse of these humanitarian convoys in order to supply military equipment and materiel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, if I am not mistaken, there was a case in which, during a regular check of a convoy, infantry ammunition was retrieved from UNHCR vehicles. I think it was in 1995. After the check, the convoy was ordered to turn back. I think Mr. Beara was present as well. We immediately asked that an official or an officer senior to us intervene. It was also recorded, I believe. The checks at Rogatica were quite rigorous. Much detail was requested. And before that occasion, nothing of the sort was found, at least nothing that would be as drastic as this example. However, as a rule, there was always a surplus of goods, or goods that were not declared, or there was technical equipment, or NATO aerial images, or navigation equipment, cameras, video cameras, surpluses of medication, flour, fuel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please, so that the witness could see who drafted the document and when. We can see on that page also that there is data concerning 1994, whereas on page 1 we had information about 1993. I seek to tender this into evidence, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is already an exhibit, is it not? Oh, I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 1D641 shall be assigned Exhibit D214. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P2126. It's footage which concerns this specific example of the ammunition found on board humanitarian convoy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "While inspecting the convoy, in about the fifth sack, I checked using a knife, I noticed there was something in the flour. When I carried out a regular inspection, I discovered the ammunition. Without a doubt, this sort of conduct represents the most serious form of criminal activity and is utterly in contrast with the mandate and nature of humanitarian missions. "Whether or not they felt caught in the act by the ammunition found in the convoy, the leader and one of the drivers reacted as follows: "I do not know anything about the ammunition found in the flour, and I have nothing to say." "I don't know where the ammunition in the truck came from. I don't know what to say. I cannot say anything, really. "Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, Colonel General Ratko Mladic, sent protests to the UNHCR offices in Zagreb, Belgrade, and Pale and asked that competent officials there take immediate measures to avoid similar incidents in the future. General Mladic also informs the UNHCR representatives about the fate of the convoy that was stopped and its personnel. General Mladic's statement said that the goods will be confiscated and appropriate legal measures taken against those responsible. "What else can we say, as we watch the images from Rogatica, that best testify to the human nature of international humanitarian organisation? Need we remind them that they have always been welcome and safe on the Serbian side in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Need we remind them that the food for the Muslim population arrives in these convoys above all because of the understanding of the Serbs? Need we remind them how many times this understanding has been abused? Should they ask themselves who has the right to transport ammunition and weapons along with food?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to thank the interpreters that they managed to interpret most of what, obviously, was said in this video footage. Thank you so much for that. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have 1D78 in e-court, which has to do with the same humanitarian convoy we saw on the footage. D78, which was marked for identification. I don't know whether it was admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In item 3, which is the fourth paragraph of the telegram, it reads: "The Ukrainian convoy," we have the number, "comprising three vehicles from Sarajevo to Zepa, passed through the check-point in Rogatica. A UNHCR convoy from Karakaj to Zepa, which arrived at the check-point yesterday, is still in Rogatica, undergoing a detailed search, since ammunition and for infantry weapons was found yesterday." Does the information in the document of the 8th of June, 1995, issued by the command of your brigade, sent to the Drina Corps, does it have to do with the convoy and the ammunition found in that convoy which moved or attempted to go through your territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I suppose it has to do with that convoy. I wasn't following the report-exchange process between the commanders. I think the brigade commander did, indeed, sign this regular combat report, though, and I think this part of it has to do with the convoy in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't start too early. I would like to know who signed this document. I would like to ask the Usher to scroll it down. And perhaps the Registrar could provide us with information why this was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document was used with the Witness Cornelis Nicolai. Since the general could not provide any precise information about the events in question or about the document itself, the document was only MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I seek to tender D78, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be now received as an exhibit, D78.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 1D640 next. It is another document of the Rogatica Brigade Command, drafted by the intelligence/security organ on the 8th of May, 1994. Mr. Carkic was there at the time. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the document I announced. It was sent to the VRS Main Staff and the Drina Corps Command. It is a report about an incident at the Rogatica check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You provide information in terms of the number of persons and vehicles, and then on the next page, page 2, you discuss the incident itself. In order to be brief, we'll look at the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just see the rest of the page, the bullet points. Could you go down, please. Yes, let's look at the paragraph just below the two names, where it says "Major Hinan Pol" and "Sergeant Rossler Murej": "Given that they became more and more insolent and that they kept protesting the checks of their vehicles and equipment, as well as picking up their weapons, I was forced to personally intervene and rely on my maximum self-control to physically persuade them to step away from the vehicle so that we could carry on. The person in charge of the convoy, a French lieutenant, Pierre [phoen], was quite fair. However, he tried to influence our decision to check the vehicles and, on a number of occasions, hindered the exercise. He requested that the military observers from Gorazde be present. It was explained to him that as the person in charge of the convoy, he made a number of mistakes and that he shouldn't make another one. Protecting the Canadians who committed the criminal offence, our French interpreter, who is a military policeman" -- I can't read the rest: "I guess he heard the leader of the convoy whisper to the Canadians. He literally said, You messed it up thoroughly."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is all about? What is the report saying? Briefly, please, so as not to waste too much time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I remember this event. And it wasn't the first time; it was just one in a line of events. I think, in this case, they failed to declare some cargo. And some Canadians appeared who were not supposed to be a part of the convoy, and they had some completely different goods from a humanitarian organisation of sorts. This is where the problem lies. The problem was with declaring those goods, and we couldn't allow it to enter Gorazde. I believe they wanted to go there. They tried to resist, and that's the gist of it. They always had this position in which they protested, and sometimes they even drew out their weapons. Some of them were quite arrogant at times, some people from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you. We have now two hours, five minutes. We must have the third break. Mr. McCloskey, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just before the document disappeared, could we see who did the document, so that had some more meaning after all that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm sure, after the break, Mr. Tolimir will use this further. I see a "Captain Zoran Carkic." Thank you. We have our third break. After the break, Judge Nyambe is not able to sit with us. The remaining Judges decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. We hoped to be able to conclude the testimony of this witness today for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom, but I would like to invite the Defence and the Prosecution to discuss how you will share this remaining time with this witness. We adjourn, and resume at 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 2.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We still have the same document on the screen that we used before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you write this document and sign it? Perhaps we can go back to the first page again.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may this be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D640 shall be assigned Exhibit D215, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, during the examination-in-chief, at page 45, line 8, you were looking at a map of Borike. There was also a place marked "IKM" there, forward command post in the village of Borike. Was it really a forward command post or merely a place where the unit was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a command post of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is Sjeversko en route to Boksanica or is it on another road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the regional road, one needs to turn to the right, towards Mount Boksanica, and then on to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it on the road between Villa Boksanica and the pass at Boksanica, where the negotiations took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not along that route. But you can get there from Borike if you turn a side road, eventually reaching Sjeversko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any Main Staff unit have its command post in Sjeversko?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean during the period of time relevant to these proceedings, I don't think there was any such unit at Sjeversko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Danko Gojkovic, the encryption person of the Rogatica Brigade, was he in charge of encoding all telegrams leaving the area of the Rogatica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I cannot confirm that. I think he was one of those in charge of encryption and that he typed out a number of documents. However, I do think other people were engaged in similar tasks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were only the codes of the Rogatica Brigade used in the documents presented by the OTP and signed by those in charge of encryption in the Rogatica Brigade? In other words, were those the only codes used?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think we used the codes of the Rogatica Brigade. As for any documents being sent by courier, that is not something I can confirm. I do suppose, however, that some documents left by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking about written documents. Concerning all the documents that had to do with the Zepa operation, did it -- did they all go through the Department for Encryption of the brigade using the same code?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether you had any wire communication. Were you shown the schematic of the Communications Department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see whether there was any wire communication with Rogatica and the commander of the brigade there, or was the only such communication between the forward command post and the Communications Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, in answer to that question, that I wasn't familiar enough with that type of communication. In any case, I did say that the schematic might be, conditionally speaking, in accordance with the principles along which the communications system was organised in the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 07305. That is the schematic. We have it. Could we please have the graphic part of the communications system of the light infantry brigade. That is page 2, I believe. Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Rogatica Brigade only have radio-relay communication with the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, it certainly did have radio-relay communication means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question was not recorded. The microphone was switched off. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. There is a schematic that the general is, I think, getting to that was reference to what the witness has been -- seen, but he -- okay, we're getting there. So that -- because I know the witness is looking for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade have only radio-relay communication with the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, as well as with the commands of its battalions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade command, as far as I know, had a radio-relay communication with it. I don't know how it functioned. I'm not familiar with the work of the signals personnel. I know that it did have an induction communication with certain units. On the front-lines there was an induction telephone line with the Communication Centre -- or, rather, among the Communications Centre there was a wire communication, as far as I know. And as far as I can remember, there was another schematic of the communications. This is not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see, in this schematic, the command post of the battalions? It says the 2nd Battalion, the 3rd Battalion, the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see that there is a radio-relay communication going to them or just a wire communication?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was a wire communication between the battalion commands and the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you see in the schematic. Do you see the radio-relay communications or the wire communications? What is it that you see?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that these are markings for the radio-relay communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please -- just a moment. Can we please move the B/C/S version to the right, and I would like to draw the witness's attention to the basic line. Would you please read that for yourself and provide us with your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The schematic of the radio-relay communications of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know the general's hurrying, but he's referred to a document that I showed the witness, I believe, in proofing. And if he's going to ask him questions about that, he should have that document, which I'm sure is very close to this one somewhere. It's page 7, which is the one he referred to, and it may make more sense, in relation to the questions he's asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would that be more helpful for your purpose, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see what it says under the schematic, the bottom sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused be asked to make breaks before -- between answers and questions or questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Everybody understands that you are now hurrying, but this is not a good communication. You shouldn't -- avoid to overlap. It is absolutely necessary to have a pause between question and answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, look at the schematic. You can see that wire communications are represented by code or lines. Would you say that those lines from the battalion commands to the positions on the front-line, is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that -- I apologise to the interpreters. Does that mean that only wire communications led from the battalion commands to the positions, whereas radio-relay communications were those that served the other communications access?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wire communications were used only for the shortest routes, the induction routes, whereas radio-relay communications were put in place between the battalion commands, the brigade commands, the Borike Forward Command Post, and the Drina Corps. In other words, there were no radio-relay communications between the battalions and their units. There were radio sets, mobile radio sets, but there were no radio communications between the battalions and companies or, rather, units on the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7305 shall be assigned Exhibit D216. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Carkic, during the examination-in-chief, you were shown a video-clip depicting General Mladic entering buses and talking to those who were seated on the buses, and they were the inhabitants of Zepa who were being evacuated. And did you hear him say at one point, Do not come back, there is a front-line in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether General Mladic singled out any of the able-bodied men? Did he tell them, There are able-bodied men among you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can hear it in the clip, that he said, There are able-bodied men among you. But I did not see him singling out anybody on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that General Mladic issued an order for the evacuation, in keeping with the agreement, had to be carried out without any incidents and that nobody had to set any conditions, save for the conditions that were set out by the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from you, not once, I heard it on several occasions from you, that the evacuation had to be carried out in an absolutely safe manner, without any extraordinary situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that because of that, during the evacuation nobody was singled out, no able-bodied were separated from the women and the children; everybody was evacuated by buses, and nobody remained in Zepa, save for the soldiers who had been in the Zepa mountain range?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I know that, but we will probably come to that part which concerns the topic that was discussed at the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm hurrying. I want us to get to that part as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, what I know and what I would like to add is what I saw, and that was that there was no separation at all. I was not aware of any separation taking place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you again said, "That's why I'm hurrying." If you need more time, you could request it and the witness will be called back. There's no need for hurrying. If you have several more questions, it will be your time. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D722 is the next document I would like to call up, page 51, lines 13 and 14. Thank you. This is page 34 in English and 51 in Serbian, in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have to tell you that this is your statement that you provided on the 22nd of February, 2011, in Rogatica, in the police station of Rogatica. Thank you. Now we can see it, lines 13 and 14, where you say, in line 13: "There were some facilities in this same zone which were destroyed by NATO. I don't see the photo here, and 10 soldiers were killed." Thank you. What did you mean when you said that? The Trial Chamber would like to know that. The sentence was taken out of the context, or, rather, it ties with what was said earlier and what will be said later, but we don't have the time to go through the entire contents of the documents.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, I was talking about two photos made from AWACS with dates that I could not provide any comment on, one of those aerial photos depicting the centre of Zepa, and all the facilities were intact, none of them were destroyed. However, the same sector, the same segment, was depicted in the second aerial photo on a date that I cannot comment upon, and in that second photo I couldn't see any of those facilities. They were simply not there. My comment was that -- or, rather, the question was what I could say about that operation. That was what the investigator asked me. He asked me what I could say about that operation, and my answer was that there hadn't been any operation and that I didn't hear anything of any such operation. And then I was told that that had been done in a planned manner, something to that effect. I couldn't confirm that because I really had never heard anybody ordering the torching or destruction of any facilities in Zepa, including the mosque that we are talking about. I know that one of the witnesses allegedly commented upon all that, and he said that he had seen some soldiers who had planted mines around the mosque, but I can't speak on his behalf because I, myself, never saw that, I was never informed about that, I don't know what soldiers those may have been. And then I was told that they were members of our brigade. I said that I'm not sure what could be the basis for somebody to claim that those were members of our brigade, because there were members of other units there as well. And, finally, when I refused to even think that that was done according to a plan, because I know that we had never received any such order during the war, and I could not accept that this -- that was done systematically, that that was a systematic destruction of any of the facilities, then I commented, and I said that in the Zepa zone there were other destroyed facilities and that one of them was the facility called Zlovrh that was hit by one, two, or three NATO bombs. And on that occasion, 10 of our soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D689 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you know about the killing of those soldiers? What do you know about that? Thank you. 1D689 is the document I've called up. This is a document issued by the Command of the 1st Drina Light Assault Brigade, dated the 13th of August, 1995. It was sent to the Drina Corps. And the title is "Regular Combat Report." It says here: "This morning, around 0230 hours, the NATO Air Force shelled a facility which had previously housed a communications centre in Zlovrh facility. The facility had been torched by Ustasha, and over the past 10 or so days it was used for the accommodation of our unit, which scoured and controlled the territory with a view to detecting and removing the remaining enemy elements." Thank you. Can you tell us whether in August 1995, the facility in Zlovrh was used as a communications centre, or did it play the role as it is described in this combat report? Did it only billet soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only used -- used to accommodate soldiers, i.e., units that had certain tasks in the Zepa zone, because it was still an very volatile period and there were some elements of armed groups still present from the Zepa Brigade. And from time to time there were exchanges of fire between our members and the remains of the Zepa Brigade who -- and those exchanges were not negligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I've switched the microphone off because I wanted that the accused waits for the end of the translation. Please continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, could you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, what were the consequences of the shelling of the facility at Zlovrh?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences are visible in the report that was sent as a regular combat report by the commander of that unit. Ten members of the unit were killed, those who used that facility for their accommodation in that zone. A few of them were wounded. I suffered contusions. Some of them still suffer the consequences of that incident. The facility was totally destroyed. The survivors had to be pulled out from the rubble. That is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this be admitted into evidence. And I would like to ask for the previous document, which was the witness's statement, to be called back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see the signature of the document we have just had on the screen. Thank you. Signed by Rajko Kusic. Thank you very much. It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 1D689 shall be assigned Exhibit D217, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before we go into private session, let's look at 1D722, 1D722, which is the witness's statement, and can we please look at page 38, lines 10 through 32. Thank you. In English, it is page 26. The lines are from 10 to 32. I'm going to read just one part of it, and then I will have questions for you. Thank you. We see line 10. Can this be blown up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote what you said: "I think -- I think his driver was with him, only his driver. It was a problem with this unit. And this actually was not an UNPROFOR unit; this was the unit for rapid intervention, composed mostly of French Legionaires, and there was perhaps one or two Russians. And the explanation differed. The French were rather arrogant." And then I move to the following line, where the sentence starts with the following words: "They took over the UNPROFOR check-point at Boksanica. They insisted on entering Zepa, allegedly because they wanted to look for the remaining civilians, although the evacuation had already ended. They didn't have the permission of the Main Staff to enter Zepa, since the combat activities were still going on in the area, because the Zepa Brigade soldiers did not want to surrender. That's why the conflicts continued from Zepa towards north and north-east." Further on, it says: "The Main Staff didn't allow that, and at some point even weapons were drawn." My question is this: Is this what you knew at the time? Was the Rapid Intervention Unit entitled to enter in the territory where combat was ongoing? Would UNPROFOR have had the same right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, whether anybody approved their arrival, I don't know. I'm not sure about that. We were told that a unit was to appear, or, rather, we knew that it was a mixed unit that was coming our way, and they did not arrive under the umbrella of UNPROFOR, as it were. At that time around Sarajevo there were already rapid intervention units, they had already been established, and that was one of them. Their conduct was very aggressive. I witnessed the situations when weapons were drawn, I saw that entire [indiscernible] equipment was put in positions. There were few of us there. At one point, I was on my own. To the left of me on the plateau or on the Boksanica Pass, there were two of our tanks. However, the crews did not even pay attention to any of that.
