I didn't even want to burden them with all of that. I wanted to -- I requested the presence from -- of someone from the Main Staff. Colonel Beara came, and he tried to talk to the French officer. He wanted to establish some sort of a normal communication. I believe that his name was Jean-Loup. However, that person did not accept any normal communication. He insisted on entering Zepa. He wanted to look for the remaining civilians, allegedly. There was still combat ongoing down there, and that combat spilled over to Boksanica Mountain or, rather, to the Zepa Plateau. Let's not confuse things. That area was called Sjemec - not Sjemic, but Sjemec - on Zepa Mountain. And that combat was going on for a while after that. The Main Staff did not want to allow anybody to enter in an area as unsafe as that, especially in view of the fact that that unit, as far as I know, did not even have the mandate to do that. The Main Staff would have been informed if they had an official mandate to enter the protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to go back to this statement, could this statement be admitted into evidence, please, given that I have used it a number of times. Could we now see just one more document, please, P486. Thank you. P486 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up: The previous document, 1D722, will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the clarity of the record, I just need to put that 1D689 was already MFI'd through General Smith as Exhibit D187. Therefore, D187 shall be assigned to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- 722. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as Mr. Gajic and I discussed, upon your request, I mentioned to him that I would like 30 minutes. That leaves the general 20, and he hasn't gotten to the area yet. But -- and I know you're very aware of all of this, so I won't say anything else, but it's looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I, myself, am quite concerned about the situation and the ongoing process. I would like to take out some speed and to enable Mr. Tolimir to have a sufficient conduct of his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we, of course, can work with both the witness and Mr. Stojanovic to find a time that they can come back that is within their schedule. I know Mr. Stojanovic well, and I know he will make every effort. And the witness has always been co-operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registrar needs to correct something on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 65 ter document 1D689 was assigned Exhibit D187, marked for identification, pending translation, through General Smith. 65 ter document 1D722 shall be assigned Exhibit D217. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means D187 is now an exhibit no longer marked for identification because we have a translation; is that correct? It's not correct. Sorry, I mixed up both the documents. Forget it, what I just said. Continue, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we see P486 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to come up, let me tell you that this document comes from the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. It was drafted on the 29th of July. I'm showing this in order to show that on the 29th of July this incident with the Frenchman happened. The document was sent to the addressees, and in the first item we see: "We had a meeting at 0800 hours with Colonel Jean-Loup, where he said the following: "He was tasked with evacuating all remaining Muslim civilians from the Zepa enclave. "While waiting for the permission of General Smith to go up in the mountains to see if there are any remaining civilians perhaps." Would you please tell us whether this pertains to that member of the Rapid Intervention Forces or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he say what he's quoted here as saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, when Mr. Pecanac had a meeting -- discussion with him, I wasn't present. I think they came perhaps on the 28th of July, because they stayed for at least two or three days up there at the check-point. And when Pecanac met with Jean-Loup, I was not present. I was present when Colonel Beara was there and prior to the arrival of Colonel Beara. However, the story was the same on both occasions, as was presented to Mr. Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have D217 placed under seal? That's the witness's statement, and there's information in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it should be admitted under seal. And I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Tolimir. You were reading, and I don't know if that is a translation matter, page 108, line 16. You were quoting from the document: "He was tasked with evacuating all remaining Muslim civilians from the Zepa enclave." In the document, we see the translation: "He was tasked to evacuate all remaining Muslims from the Zepa enclave," without the word "civilians." There is a difference. Perhaps it's a translation issue. I don't know. Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the original document, it says "civilians from the Muslim enclave of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should I confirm, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the first bullet point, it says: "He was tasked to evacuate all remaining Muslims ..." And is there a reference to Muslim civilians or not in the B/C/S version, in the Serbian text? Thank you. With the assistance of the Usher, we saw the word "civilians." Thank you. There's no need for a confirmation. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have this document admitted into evidence. And could we also moved into closed session so that I can finish with my part of cross-examination by the agreed dead-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is already in evidence, P486. We turn into a private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that given the likelihood that Zlovrh was going to be targeted by NATO, that it was a bad idea to have soldiers billeted there that were doing a search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the matter for the command function. It turned out that it was a bad idea, but we did not have the information that Zlovrh would be bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, the information was certainly before General Mladic, so the information should have come from the Main Staff or from the Drina Corps that you should keep your men away from major targets, shouldn't it have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier today we saw a document where it says that Zlovrh was not a communications centre, that the Muslims had torched it before their withdrawal, and that it was only used to billet troops. I don't know what is the basis for forcing the witness to give an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we put the next document on the ELMO. It specifically responses to General Tolimir's concern. It is a bill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- from the Drina Corps in the amount of US$540.000 to recover the destruction of the repeater at Zlovrh as a result of NATO bombing. I have a couple of English versions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient to have it on the ELMO. It will have to be translated -- oh, you have the English translation. Yes, that would be helpful for the Defence and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Defence -- it should have both languages in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart can give it number 7329. And we can see that this is from the Drina Corps to the army, the Main Staff, and it says, "Reasons and Consequences of the Enemy Activities: Submission." And then we can see that it goes on to review the consequences of NATO aviation, and it says: "Report. Losses of manpower and assessment of material damage caused by NATO aviation activities: Ten combatant soldiers perished due to NATO aviation activities, one of them a fighter squad commander." That may be the gentleman that did not get warned by their security officers from the Zvornik -- from the Rogatica Brigade. "B. The material damage to the facilities caused by NATO aviation activities is as follows:" It talks about the warehouses, the bridge, the repeater at Trover [sic] facility -- the repeater at Zlovrh facility, US$540.000, and then material damage together is an enormous --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would this repeater be a fair military target, in your view, if, in fact, a $540.000 repeater was blown up by NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a question for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm aware that we are in open session at the moment, and here, this is a very heavy comment addressed at me and about me. If I understood Mr. Peter properly, he said that I, who knew about the bombing of Zlovrh, did not inform the men who were billeted there. At least that's what I heard in the earphones. If that is correct, then I'm speechless, if the interpretation was the correct interpretation of the Prosecutor's words. If that was said, under such pressure, I can no longer function. Because if somebody accuses me, be it even through a commentary, before my people, before the army that I belonged to, if somebody is accusing me of not having conveyed the information that Zlovrh would be bombed and I knew that it would happen, and that's completely untrue, then I am asking for this to be withdrawn and to be denied, because I didn't know that. I've not seen this document before in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not the question Mr. McCloskey put to you. He wanted to know if this would be a legitimate military target if there was installed such a repeater. That was the question. It doesn't have anything to do with your personal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And just to clarify it: I'd asked you if you'd known, and you said you weren't sure. And then I said that the Main Staff had received the information. So it's on the record that you weren't sure about that. And your duty to report things that you're not sure on, I don't know, and so I'm not commenting any further. And now my question is very simple: Is this a military target, a fair military target?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would put the question in a different way. Did you know that there was such a repeater with this -- yeah, that you would need this amount of money to buy a new one? Did you know that such a repeater was installed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that repeater used to be the central repeater of the Yugoslav People's Army. And I dare say it even covered the entire area of Yugoslavia. And that would be the answer to your first question. Secondly, I didn't say that I wasn't sure that the repeater existed in Zlovrh or, rather, whether the former, previously-destroyed repeater was a legitimate target of NATO air force. I said that I didn't have information to the effect that the repeater would be bombed. Thirdly, allegedly General Mladic did know that the repeater would be bombed. We, ourselves, did not have that information. In other words, I did not have that information ever. I should have been only so lucky to have had it, because I could have saved the lives of ten of my comrades. And what has now happened to me here is really unheard of. And, fourthly, I absolutely don't know how much things cost. I never saw any documents regarding the estimates of the cost of damages on the repeater. I was never in charge of any such thing. Please, as the Presiding Judge, could you please protect me from any insinuations from any side? Can you imagine how it is going to be for me to come back to Rogatica after it was said that I knew that Rogatica and Zlovrh would be bombed? And I never knew that. Do you know what it means for me to come and face the families of my dead colleagues? This is unheard of. I'm sorry, I'm acting very emotionally, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, and there was no need for that, because nobody in this courtroom made this insinuation. It was something else. You were asked if you knew that, and you denied that, and that was all, in relation to your personal position. Mr. McCloskey referred to knowledge, alleged knowledge, of General Mladic. This is something totally different from you. And I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey not to ask him legal questions. I think he is not the appropriate witness to decide if that was a legitimate target for NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Your question was better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if something is stated that concerns the witness personally, could, in the future, a reference be provided testifying to the fact whether the witness knew something or not or whether the Main Staff knew something or not? I don't want things to be said arbitrarily. If Mr. McCloskey says that Zlovrh was a legitimate target, then he should say why. We know that General Smith said before this Trial Chamber that the Security Council had never allowed him to bomb any of the facilities in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now a statement, and we should avoid discussions about legal matters among the parties in the presence of a witness who should be asked about his knowledge and the facts he knows about. Mr. McCloskey, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was given a 65 ter number just now. It will be received. But I have only the translation of the first page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that is correct. We'll -- we didn't do the whole thing, and we should mark it for identification and get the whole thing done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Registry would appreciate if we can be provided with a hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will give you my hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7329 shall be assigned Exhibit P2177. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, you had said earlier, I have it on page 63 -- and I think you agreed with General Tolimir when he mentioned that the transfer of the people from Zepa was meant to be temporary and that 300 houses had been reconstructed, that people have -- some have moved back, at least for weekend homes. And you talked a bit about no organised process or operation to destroy houses. Can we now look at something I know you have seen before, 65 ter 7328, page 2. If we could make this a full size. This is something that we got from the US relatively recently. We'd provided copies to the Defence when we got it. It's an aerial image of 24 August of north-east Zepa. And on it, the United States has identified, in boxes, buildings that were destroyed since 27 July 1995. And this is just a portion. I can go over the mosque area, I can go over other parts of the towns, and we still -- we see this massive destruction of houses. And I can show you the photographs from July 27th that show those houses intact. I know you've seen them before, because you were shown them in the interview. So -- and the person you're referring to in the testimony was a person that was from your brigade that saw the mosque blown up with mines and saw these houses being destroyed. So, sir, in looking at this, knowing these places were destroyed sometime after July 27th, do you really -- do you want to testify, sir, that you were aware of no operation to destroy all these houses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do wish to testify that. And I confirm I did not know about any operation of destroying houses and mosques. And I'm repeating this for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to page 1. Perhaps we can put them both up so there can be a comparison, though I will have larger photographs for the Court, if they wish to look. It's really hard to tell. Can we just blow up the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You'll agree with me, in this 27 July shot we see a lot of roofs that are intact, don't we?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer these aerial images into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P2178 shall be assigned to these documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's a dispute about the number? No. Okay. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Carkic, General Tolimir spent quite a bit of time talking about this ambush on the Serb soldiers that was -- happened in the beginning of the war, and he referred to it as a murder and a terrible thing, and the loss of life always is. But let me briefly outline to you what a Muslim soldier and a teacher at primary school -- his account, and just get your view, and this will be the last question or series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the statement is at 65 ter 7327, and page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This person is from Zepa and is giving an account of how things were, and I'll just start at the relevant part: "On the 6th of May, there was the first attack on the villages which were close to the local community Borike. Borike was inhabited completely by Serbs, and the attack came from there. Three Muslim villages were attacked that day, Godimlje, Zivaljevici, and Stara Gora. The inhabitants were expelled, and all the houses were burned down, and two mosques in Godimlje and Stara Gora were completely destroyed. The inhabitants came to Zepa, and we realised that Zepa might get attacked as well, so we started to organise the defence. In that same period, the Muslim villages around Rogatica were also attacked, and a lot of refugees came from those villages -- came to Zepa as well. The inhabitants of the village Djile, from the municipality of Vlasenica, were attacked, and the refugees came from there to Zepa also. In the beginning of June, villages in Han Pijesak municipality were also attacked." Now, this is the paragraph I want to ask you about: "On 4 June, there was the first attack on Zepa from Han Pijesak. A courier from the VRS had brought a message to the commander of the army in Zepa, asking permission for VRS army vehicles to come through Zepa to take food supplies to the position at Zlovrh. The commander gave permission only for food, but only [sic] for one big convoy of 40 vehicles, vehicles with soldiers, and with a tank leading them, arrived at a village called Brloznik, at the entrance to Zepa. It was realised that this was to be an attack on Zepa. The convoy passed through the village, which is situated in a narrow canyon. Our army unit made a barricade on the road, which stopped the convoy, and then fighting started. The fighting went on all day, and when the Serb units realised they could not enter Zepa, aircraft arrived. Late in the afternoon, the aircraft started bombing civilian targets in the villages around Zepa as well as the centre of Zepa itself." So, to your knowledge, were there several armoured vehicles and a very large convoy that was going through to deliver food?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at that time, I was in Sarajevo, so all that I said concerning the incident in Budicin Potok, I spoke from what I know. What I know is only in general terms, and I just conveyed what I knew. I heard other people say that that unit was announced. They were heading for their base at Zlovrh. They were carrying food and equipment. I don't know their combat structure and disposition. All I know is that on that occasion 40 to 45 men were killed and others were wounded or taken prisoner. As for the composition of that column of men and vehicles, I don't know. I don't know if there was one or two tanks or any armoured vehicles. Maybe there were some, but I don't think that any aircraft were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, given that your -- as you said, your testimony appears to be based on second-hand knowledge and information from the village of those that, unfortunately, lost their loved ones, I think we can leave it at that. And just to be clear, sir, I'm not saying you had knowledge of the bombing of Zlovrh. I asked you if you did, and you said you didn't, I guess. And you certainly were not involved in shelling the civilian population in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on that, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please state who was the witness who gave the statement, and when the statement was given?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and I can offer that into evidence or not. His name is Ramiz Dedic. It is a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, an interviewer named Steve Upton, and it was done on 27 June 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Will he be called as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It was just the -- it was the depth and the breadth and the importance that General Tolimir gave to that subject that got us looking for material, and we found this, and that's why I wanted to just bring out the other side of the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's no need to tender it, because you read the relevant part into the transcript. The document we have received, D118, marked for identification, pending translation, should be under seal. 218, yes. Oh, I misspoke. D218, MFI, that should be under seal. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm very sorry, I have a final question. Mr. McCloskey spoke about Zepa and the conditions of people if they would come back. You told us this morning, on page 63, line 14, that there was a returnee project initiated. When was that initiated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CARKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about that, I was referring to a project that is parts of the framework agreement for peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's the Project of Repatriation. That is an ongoing project in our area. I also said that property laws have been put in place, whereas repatriation and reconstruction is something that is moving ahead with difficulty, but it's going on. Houses are being rebuilt, and I'm organising these projects in the course of my duties. And it would have been preposterous for me to have destroyed these houses in order to rebuild them now. I am not aware of their destruction, or any strategy or plan of destruction, or any military assignment to that effect. I've already said what I had to say about that, and I'm not going to repeat it. I guarantee that nobody stood behind such a so-called operation, nobody ordered any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was your final answer. I would like to thank many people; first of all, the interpreters, the whole staff, court recorder, who were so patient with us, including the security people. That was for the benefit of the witness. And, therefore, I think it was an exhaustive exercise for you today; it was a very long session. But now you are able to return to your normal activities and will be able to stay with your family. Mr. Tolimir, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry, I was -- I had my hand up even earlier. I don't want to have the last word after you, but this last statement offered by the Prosecutor for admission is also hearsay because that witness says, The next day, fighting continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution didn't tender this document, and, therefore, there's no need to discuss that any further. This concludes the hearing of today and your testimony. You are now free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for all you were able to testify about and that you came here to The Hague. Thank you very much, and I hope, with the assistance of your counsel, we managed not to reveal certain parts of your testimony. Thank you very much. We have to adjourn immediately because the tapes are running out. And we resume on Monday at 2.15, and hopefully in Courtroom III. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of April, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.
